title: Daily Mental Health Checklist
description: A once-a-day pass over the basics that hold a mood steady: food, water, movement, people, rest. Use it to see what you have already covered today and what is still missing.
items: Check-in with your emotions — How am I feeling today?
Stay hydrated and nourished — Have I eaten and drunk enough water?
Move my body — Did I engage in any physical activity (stretching, walking, etc.)?
Connect with others — Did I interact with someone in a meaningful way?
Practice mindfulness — Did I pause and take deep breaths or meditate?
Limit social media/news exposure — Did I avoid excessive negative content?
Engage in an enjoyable activity — Did I do something I love?
Get adequate rest — Am I prioritizing sleep and relaxation?

title: Recognizing Warning Signs
description: Helps you notice the shifts that tend to arrive before a harder stretch, like broken sleep, pulling away from people, or a mood that will not lift. It is for catching a pattern early, never for putting a label on yourself.
items: Persistent sadness or mood shifts — Have I felt low for two weeks or more?
Loss of motivation — Am I struggling with tasks that used to feel easy?
Changes in appetite or sleep — Am I sleeping too much or too little?
Increased stress or anxiety — Am I constantly overwhelmed?
Avoidance behavior — Am I withdrawing from friends, work, or activities?
Self-critical or negative thoughts — Do I frequently feel hopeless?
Physical symptoms — Have I noticed headaches, tension, or fatigue linked to stress?

title: Coping & Self-Care Strategies
description: A menu of things that help when a day turns heavy, from breathing and grounding to telling someone. Pick one or two that fit the moment rather than working down the whole list.
items: Journaling — Write down thoughts to process emotions.
Therapeutic exercises — Use structured worksheets or grounding techniques.
Breathing practices — Try box breathing or the 4-7-8 method.
Sensory grounding — Engage with sights, sounds, and textures to stay present.
Social support — Talk to a friend, therapist, or support group.
Routine setting — Create stability with morning and evening rituals.
Affirmations — Challenge negative thoughts with empowering statements.
Professional help — Seek guidance if symptoms persist or worsen.

title: Long-Term Mental Wellness Practices
description: The slower habits that keep you well over months rather than hours: boundaries, hobbies, reflection and community. Come back to it whenever you want to see where the balance has drifted.
items: Develop healthy boundaries — Say no when needed.
Nurture hobbies — Engage in activities that bring joy.
Schedule time for reflection — Regular check-ins on progress.
Educate yourself — Learn about mental health to reduce stigma.
Volunteer or engage with community — Giving back can boost well-being.
Prioritize balance — Avoid burnout by adjusting workload and self-care.

title: Steadying Yourself When Nerves Hit
description: For the twenty minutes before something that matters — an interview, a scan, a hard conversation. It walks you through settling your body first, then your head, so the nerves have somewhere to go besides your chest.
items: Name it plainly — Say “I am nervous” rather than “something is wrong with me.”
Slow the out-breath — In for four, out for six, six rounds; the long exhale is the part that settles you.
Put both feet flat on the floor — Press down and let the ground take your weight for a moment.
Find five things you can see — Naming them moves your attention out of your head and into the room.
Drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw — Nerves gather there first, and letting go tells your body the danger is not here.
Drink some water — A dry mouth and a racing heart both ease a little with a few slow sips.
Ask what you are preparing for — Nerves usually mean something matters to you, not that it will go badly.
Plan the first thirty seconds — Know your opening line or first step so you are not deciding it while shaking.

title: Winding Down for the Evening
description: A short evening routine for closing the day instead of letting it trail off into midnight. Each line is one small signal to your body and mind that nothing more is being asked of them tonight.
items: Set a stop time for work — Pick the hour the day ends and let the unfinished things stay unfinished.
Write down tomorrow’s first three things — On paper, so your mind can stop holding the list for you.
Lower the lights an hour before bed — Dim light is the oldest signal there is that the day is closing.
Put the phone in another room — Distance works where willpower does not.
Do one slow thing — A shower, a stretch, a few pages, a cup of tea; something with no goal attached.
Let the room get cool and dark — A cooler, darker room makes falling asleep easier than trying harder does.
Park the worries on paper — When your head starts up, write the thought down and tell it you will look tomorrow.
Go to bed at about the same time — A steady hour does more for your sleep than one perfect night.

title: Getting Out of Bed on a Heavy Morning
description: For the mornings when getting up feels like more than you have in you. It breaks the first hour into pieces small enough to do one at a time, starting before your feet touch the floor.
items: Let the first thought be kind — Say “this is a hard morning,” not “what is wrong with me.”
Sit up before you decide anything — Deciding whether to get up is much harder lying down.
Put your feet on the floor for ten seconds — That is the whole goal for now; standing can wait.
Open one curtain — Daylight on your face starts the clock on feeling awake.
Drink the glass of water first — Thirst makes a heavy morning heavier, and it is one easy win.
Lower the bar out loud — Name the two things that actually have to happen today, and let the rest go.
Move for two minutes — A slow stretch or a walk to the door shifts something that thinking about it will not.
Tell one person you are up — A short message gives the morning a witness and makes tomorrow easier.

title: Saying No Without Talking Yourself Out of It
description: For the moment someone asks for something and you can feel yourself about to agree anyway. It takes you from buying a minute through the actual words, so the no comes out short, kind and final.
items: Buy yourself a minute — Say “let me check and come back to you” before anything else.
Name what saying yes would cost — An evening, a weekend, or the thing you already promised someone else.
Check whose problem you are solving — If it was never yours to carry, that is your answer.
Write the no in one line — Short is kinder than a paragraph of reasons that invites negotiation.
Leave the apology out — “I can’t take that on” does not need a sorry in front of it.
Offer a smaller version only if you mean it — A half-yes you resent costs more than a clean no.
Send it before you soften it — Rereading a fair no ten times only makes it wobble.
Expect the discomfort and wait it out — Guilt after a good boundary fades; resentment after a bad yes does not.

title: Taking the Edge Off Sunday Night
description: For the Sunday-evening slump, when the week ahead starts pressing in before it has even begun. It gives the dread something concrete to do with itself, so the evening belongs to you rather than to Monday.
items: Call it dread, not a warning — Sunday nerves are a mood, not a forecast of how the week will go.
Ask what you are actually dreading — It is usually one meeting or one person, not the whole week.
Look at the real calendar — Ten seconds of facts beats an hour of imagining what is on it.
Write Monday’s first task on paper — One known starting point takes the vagueness out of the morning.
Sort one small thing out tonight — Lay out clothes, pack the bag, find the train fare; that is one less thing to carry.
Close the work apps on your phone — A notification on Sunday evening is Monday arriving early.
Put something you like in the evening — A show, a bath, a phone call; the hours left are still yours.
Set a bedtime and keep it — A late Sunday is what makes Monday as rough as you feared it would be.

title: When Anger Arrives Fast
description: For the moments anger lands before you have had a chance to think — a rude message, a plan wrecked, someone talking over you. It buys back the minute your body needs before you say something you cannot take back.
items: Say nothing for sixty seconds — Nothing you say in the first minute beats what you would say later.
Put the phone down — A reply typed in this state is a message you will be apologizing for.
Leave the room if you can — Distance brings the volume down faster than arguing your way to calm.
Breathe out longer than you breathe in — The long exhale is what tells your body the fight is off.
Unclench your hands and your jaw — Anger holds on in the body, and letting go there reaches the rest of you.
Name the line that got crossed — Anger usually means one thing: disrespect, unfairness, or being ignored.
Decide what you actually want — An apology, a change, to be heard; aim at that rather than at winning.
Go back to it when your hands are steady — The conversation will keep; the damage from having it now will not.

title: A Weekend With No One in It
description: For the long, quiet weekend when nobody has called and the hours stretch out. It works on the two halves separately: making the time bearable now, and putting one thread out so next weekend has something in it.
items: Say it is loneliness, not a verdict — An empty weekend is a gap in the calendar, not proof about you.
Get out among people once — A coffee shop, a library, a store; being near others counts even without talking.
Send one message you would normally not send — “Thinking of you, how are things?” is enough to start.
Put a shape on the day — One thing in the morning and one in the afternoon; empty hours get heavier.
Move for twenty minutes — A walk changes the day more than another hour of scrolling will.
Notice who you scroll past — Watching other people’s weekends is not the same as having one.
Do one thing you would do for a guest — Cook properly, open the window, put music on; you count as company.
Put one thing on the calendar for next week — A class, a call, a coffee; loneliness eases through plans, not willpower.

title: When Money Worry Won’t Switch Off
description: For the nights the numbers keep circling and nothing gets decided. It turns the vague dread into facts, one next step and a time to stop, so the worry has somewhere to go besides 3 am.
items: Write the actual number down — A known figure is easier to face than the one your head keeps rounding up.
Separate this week from this year — Most money dread is a far-off problem borrowing tonight’s attention.
Name the very next step — One call, one form, one email; not the whole way out.
Give it a slot tomorrow — Worry lets go a little once it has an appointment.
Find out what help exists — Payment plans, hardship terms and free advice lines are more common than people think.
Tell one person the real picture — Money worry gets heavier in private than it ever is out loud.
Stop checking the balance tonight — Looking again after hours changes nothing and costs you the sleep.
Do one kind ordinary thing — Tea, a shower, a walk; being broke is not a reason to go without comfort.

title: The Week After a Loss
description: For the first days after someone has died, when ordinary life keeps asking things of you. It holds the bar at eating, resting and letting people help, and asks nothing of you beyond that.
items: Eat something every few hours — Grief empties the tank, and forgetting to eat makes all of it harder.
Drink water and lie down — Your body is doing heavy work even when you are sitting still.
Decide nothing big this week — No moves, no clearing out, no promises; they will all keep.
Give one person a real job — A meal, a ride, a call made on your behalf; people want something to do.
Say no to what you cannot face — Turning down a gathering is allowed, and it needs no explanation.
Let the crying come when it comes — Grief does not keep to a schedule, and holding it back costs more.
Keep one thread of routine — A shower, a walk, feeding the cat; one fixed point steadies a shapeless day.
Reach out if it turns very dark — If you are thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 at any hour.

title: When the Inner Critic Gets Loud
description: For the hours after a mistake, when the voice in your head starts summing up your whole character. It gets the accusation out where you can look at it, then tests it against what actually happened.
items: Write the sentence down word for word — On paper it reads like the accusation it is, not like the truth.
Name the voice as a voice — “My critic is saying I am useless” puts a little air between you and it.
Ask if you would say it to a friend — If it would be cruel out loud, it is cruel in your head too.
Look for the actual evidence — One bad meeting is not a career, and one snapped reply is not a character.
Ask what it is trying to protect — The critic usually believes it is keeping you from failing in public.
Say the fair version instead — Not “I am wonderful”, just what a decent witness would say about today.
Do one small competent thing — Action argues with the critic better than reasoning with it does.
Tell someone what it has been saying — Said out loud to someone kind, it loses most of its size.

title: Coming Down From a Panic Wave
description: For the twenty minutes after panic crests, when your body is still racing and you feel wrung out. It sees you through the tail end without fighting it, and says what to do with the rest of the day.
items: Tell yourself it is cresting, not building — Panic climbs, peaks and falls on its own; this is the falling part.
Stop trying to stop it — Fighting the feeling adds a second alarm on top of the first.
Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in — The long exhale is what brings your heart rate back down.
Put your back against something solid — A wall or a chair gives your body a fixed edge to find.
Name what is around you out loud — Five things you see, four you hear; it pulls attention out of your chest.
Let your hands warm up — Warm water or pockets; cold hands are the adrenaline leaving, not danger.
Eat and drink something afterward — A wave burns through you, and the shakiness afterward is partly empty fuel.
Lower the bar for the rest of the day — You have just been through something; nothing more is owed today.
Know where the extra help is — If panic is shaping your week, a professional helps; if you ever feel unsafe, call or text 988.

title: Starting When You Cannot Focus
description: For the afternoon you have read the same paragraph four times and opened nothing. It shrinks the job until starting is easy, then removes the things pulling your attention away.
items: Write down the one thing that matters today — A list of nine competing jobs is why nothing has started.
Cut it down to ten minutes’ worth — Not the whole report, just the first paragraph, small enough to feel boring.
Put the phone in another room — Willpower loses to a screen within reach every time.
Close every tab but one — Each open tab is a small ongoing decision about where to look.
Set a timer and work badly on purpose — A rough first pass beats a perfect one you never begin.
Write down the distracting thought — On a scrap of paper it stops circling and waits its turn.
Stand up and move at the timer — Focus comes back faster after two minutes away than after an hour of pushing.
Note where you stopped — A half-finished sentence is the easiest place in the world to start again.

title: When You Are the One Holding It Together
description: For anyone looking after someone who needs a great deal, on the weeks it is all invisible. It puts your own name on the list, asks for help in a way people can actually answer, and makes room for the resentment.
items: Name what only you are doing — The appointments, the worry, the decisions made alone all count as work.
Ask for one specific thing this week — “Can you sit with her Thursday?” lands where “let me know if you need anything” never does.
Put your own appointment on the calendar — The dentist, the checkup, the haircut; caregivers postpone these for years.
Eat one real meal sitting down — Standing at the counter between tasks does not count as eating.
Take twenty minutes outside — Not an errand and not productive; twenty minutes that belong to you.
Let something slip on purpose — Choose what drops rather than finding out when it breaks.
Say the resentment out loud somewhere safe — Loving someone and being worn out by them sit together fine.
Find one person in the same boat — A support group or a friend who gets it beats explaining from scratch.

title: The First Day Back After Time Away
description: For the morning you return to a full inbox and the break already feels undone. It gets you through the first day without losing what the time off gave you, and keeps the pile from setting the terms.
items: Start an hour later if you can — Beginning the day before the inbox opens is easier than beginning inside it.
Read everything before replying to anything — Half of what looked urgent sorted itself out while you were gone.
Write down the three things that matter — A pile is not a list until you have turned it into one.
Turn down the first new request — Whatever arrives on day one can wait until you have your footing.
Keep one thing from the time away — The walk, the early night, the book; one habit is worth carrying back.
Expect to feel behind and slow — The first day always feels like this; it is not a verdict on the break.
Finish one small thing before lunch — One completed item does more for the day than three half-started ones.
Leave on time today — Working late on day one sets the terms for the whole week.

title: Before a Conversation You Have Been Dreading
description: For the talk you have rehearsed in your head for weeks and still have not had. It sorts out what you actually want from it, gives you an opening line, and sets the bar somewhere you can reach.
items: Write down what you want to come out of it — An apology, a change, an answer; pick one, not all three.
Cut it to one sentence — If you cannot say the point in a sentence, the conversation will wander.
Decide your opening line and keep it — The first ten seconds are the hardest, so do not improvise them.
Lead with what you noticed, not what they are — “The last three Fridays” goes somewhere; “you always” does not.
Plan for them not taking it well — You are not responsible for managing their reaction as well as your own.
Pick a time when neither of you is running — Not bedtime, not out the door, not over a meal you cooked.
Decide what you will not get into — Name the old argument you are not reopening today.
Set the bar at saying it, not at winning — Having said the thing out loud is the whole success here.

title: Getting Back to Moving Your Body
description: For the restart after weeks or years away, when the old routine feels out of reach and starting feels faintly humiliating. It sets the first week absurdly low on purpose, so there is a second week.
items: Pick something you do not dread — The best exercise is whichever one you will still be doing in March.
Make the first session laughably short — Ten minutes is plenty; the point this week is going, not the workout.
Put it in the calendar twice — Two named slots beat a vague plan to go more often.
Get the clothes out the night before — Removing one small obstacle decides more mornings than motivation does.
Go at a pace you could talk at — Starting too hard is the most common way a restart ends in week one.
Expect to feel unfit and go anyway — That feeling is the starting line, not a sign you should not be here.
Skip the comparison to your old self — You are not behind; you are at the beginning, which is a different thing.
Notice one thing that felt better — Sleep, mood, looser shoulders; that is the reason worth keeping.

title: Parenting on Almost No Sleep
description: For the stretch when the nights are broken and the days run on fumes. It drops the standard to feeding and safety, finds you an hour off, and takes the short temper off your conscience.
items: Lower today to feeding and safety — Everything else on the list genuinely keeps until you have slept.
Take the nap that is offered — Twenty minutes now beats a tidy kitchen you will not remember.
Eat something without waiting to sit down — Standing over the sink still counts on a day like this.
Get outside for ten minutes — Daylight and air do more for a foggy head than another coffee.
Hand over an hour and actually leave — Hovering in the next room is not a break for anyone.
Forgive the short temper — Snapping on two hours of sleep is a tired body, not the parent you are.
Pick one thing to undo the chaos — The dishes or the floor, not both; one visible win is enough today.
Ask for help before you are desperate — Help arranged on an ordinary day arrives faster than help begged for on a bad one.

title: When the House Has Got Away From You
description: For the rooms that piled up during a hard stretch, when the whole job looks too big to start. It gives you fifteen minutes, one surface and no decisions, which is how a house actually gets climbed back out of.
items: Start with a trash bag, not a plan — Throwing out needs no decisions and clears the most space fastest.
Set a timer for fifteen minutes — The goal is to stop on time, not to finish the house.
Do one surface, not one room — A cleared table you can see changes the feel of everything around it.
Run the dishwasher or the laundry first — Machines do their part while you do yours.
Put like with like before deciding anything — Sorting is easier than choosing, and it shows you the real size of it.
Leave the sentimental box for another day — It is the slowest pile and it will stall you every time.
Keep a donation bag by the door — Anything undecided goes in; if it is not missed in a month, it goes for good.
Skip the guilt about how it got here — A house gets away from people during hard stretches, and this is the climb out.

title: Getting Through an Event You Dread
description: For the party, wedding or work thing you already want to get out of. It gives you an exit time, something to do with your hands and your mouth, and a definition of success you can actually meet.
items: Decide your leaving time before you go — Knowing you can leave at nine is what makes the first hour possible.
Arrive early rather than late — Walking into six people is far easier than walking into sixty.
Have two questions ready — People like being asked things, and it takes the talking off you.
Find the job nobody wants — Pouring drinks or minding the door gives you a reason to be standing there.
Take the break you need — Five minutes alone outside or in the bathroom resets more than pushing through.
Let the silences belong to both of you — A pause is shared; it is not evidence about you.
Skip the replay on the way home — The post-event audit is the worst part of the night and the least accurate.
Count going as the win — You went; whether you shone is a different and far less important question.

title: Taking a Day Off Without Earning It
description: For the rest you keep postponing until you have done enough to deserve it. It protects the day from errands and guilt, and settles what counts as a good one before it starts.
items: Book it before you feel you deserve it — Waiting to earn rest is how people end up never resting.
Tell one person it is a day off — Said out loud, it is harder to quietly fill with errands.
Leave the to-do list in another room — A rest day with the list in sight is not a rest day.
Pick one thing you actually want to do — Not improving, not catching up; wanting it is the whole test.
Let the day be unproductive on purpose — That is not the day going wrong, that is the day working.
Notice the guilt and carry on anyway — Guilt on a day off is a habit, not information.
Keep the phone out of the first hour — The day is more yours if it does not open with other people’s needs.
Do not make up for it tomorrow — Rest paid back with a double shift was a loan, not a rest.

title: When Worry Wakes You in the Night
description: For the small hours, when one thought has you wide awake and everything looks unfixable. It gets the worry out of your head, decides nothing until daylight, and stops the night turning into a second problem.
items: Blame the hour, not yourself — At three in the morning everything looks unsolvable; that is the hour talking.
Write the worry on paper by the bed — On the page it stops needing to be held in your head.
Ask whether anything can be done now — If the answer is no, this is rumination rather than problem-solving.
Promise it a hearing in daylight — The worry will keep until morning, when you will be better equipped for it.
Get up if twenty minutes pass — Lying there awake teaches your body that bed is a place for worrying.
Keep the lights low and the screen off — Bright light tells your body it is morning when it is not.
Do something dull on purpose — A boring book or a slow stretch beats lying still and thinking.
Skip the clock arithmetic — Working out how little sleep is left only adds a second worry to the first.

title: Before You Ask for a Raise
description: For the week before you finally bring up pay. It gets your case onto one page, settles the number before you are in the room, and decides ahead of time what a no will mean.
items: Write down what you have actually done — Specific wins carry further than a general sense of working hard.
Find out what the work pays elsewhere — A number with a source behind it is harder to wave away.
Name your figure before the meeting — Deciding in the room means deciding under pressure.
Say the number out loud a few times — The first time should not be in front of your manager.
Ask for the meeting in writing — A booked conversation is harder for either of you to keep postponing.
Lead with the work, not your costs — Rent going up is true, but it is not the case for your value.
Let the silence sit after you ask — The pause is uncomfortable and it is not your job to fill it.
Decide in advance what a no means — Ask again in six months, or start looking; know which before you go in.

title: After a Fight With Someone You Love
description: For the hour or two after it, when the house is quiet and you are still rehearsing your side. It settles you first, then sorts out what is worth coming back to and how to open the door again.
items: Give it twenty minutes before anything else — Nothing useful gets said while both of you are still flooded.
Drink water and go to a different room — Your body comes down faster when the scene changes.
Write your side out, for you only — On paper it loses the heat it has in your head.
Find the one sentence underneath it — Usually it is “I felt dismissed” or “I felt alone”, not the dishes.
Name one thing they got right — Not a concession; just the part of their case that holds.
Decide what you are apologizing for — Your own share, specifically, with no “but” attached to it.
Open with repair, not with the argument — “I hate it when we are like this” goes further than a better point.
Agree when you will come back to it — Some things need a calmer hour, not the same night.

title: Studying When the Exam Is Close
description: For the last stretch before a test, when panic makes you reread the same pages for hours. It swaps rereading for recall, protects sleep as part of the work, and keeps the days before from eating you.
items: Write what is actually on the exam — Vague dread covers more ground than the syllabus does.
Close the notes and test yourself — Trying to recall it teaches more than reading it again.
Work in blocks with real breaks — Forty minutes on, ten minutes properly off, beats four blurred hours.
Start with what you avoid — The topic you keep skipping is usually the one costing you points.
Make the hard bit smaller — One formula, one case, one date; progress needs a size you can hold.
Protect sleep as part of studying — A tired brain cannot retrieve what a rested one knows.
Eat and move once during the day — Studying through hunger makes the next hour slower, not longer.
Stop at a set time tonight — An open-ended evening of panic studying does less than a planned one.

title: Before a Medical Appointment That Frightens You
description: For the days before a scan, a test result or a visit you have been putting off. It helps you get your questions down, bring someone with you, and sit in the waiting room without the fear filling every hour until then.
items: Write your three biggest questions on your phone — having them in front of you means the ones that matter get asked.
Note when your symptoms started and what changes them — that answer is hard to assemble on the spot.
Ask one person to come with you or be on call — a second set of ears catches what you will not hear.
Pack water, a snack and something to read — waiting is easier when your body is not also hungry.
Say out loud what frightens you most about today — naming it leaves you with one worry instead of all of them.
Put both feet flat on the floor in the waiting room — a steady base gives your body something solid to hold.
Ask the doctor to write down what you must remember — notes carry better than a memory that is already busy.
Decide what you will do straight after the visit — a plan for the next hour keeps the day from stopping there.

title: Your First Therapy Session
description: For the week before you first sit down with a therapist. It helps you work out what you want to say, what you want to ask them, and how to get through the first hour without feeling you have to perform.
items: Write the one thing you most want to change — a single starting point is easier than a whole history.
Jot down when it started and what you have already tried — it saves you telling the story twice.
Check how you get there and leave ten minutes spare — arriving rushed costs you the start of the hour.
Ask what their approach is and how long it usually takes — you are allowed to understand the plan you are in.
Say at the start if you find it hard to talk — a therapist can work with that once they know.
Decide what you would rather not cover yet — you set the pace, and saying so is part of the work.
Keep the hour after it free — what comes up often lands once you are back outside.
Note one thing afterward that felt useful or off — it tells you whether this is the right fit.

title: When a Friend Is Struggling
description: For when someone you care about is having a hard time and you are not sure what to say. It helps you offer something concrete, ask the question people avoid asking, and keep enough of yourself back that you can stay in it.
items: Send one short message with no question in it — it tells them you are there without asking for a reply.
Offer one specific thing instead of anything you need — a named offer is far easier to accept.
Ask how they are doing, then wait through the pause — the real answer usually comes second.
Ask directly whether they are thinking of suicide — the question does not plant the idea, and it opens the door.
Save 988 in your phone and theirs — call or text reaches a crisis counselor any hour of the day.
Say plainly that you do not have the answer — honesty is better company than advice.
Set a reminder to check back in three days — being remembered later matters more than the first call.
Tell one other person what you are carrying — holding someone up works better when you are not alone.

title: Putting the Phone Down Mid-Scroll
description: For the half hour that disappears into bad news and other people's lives. It helps you notice you are scrolling, break the loop without deleting everything, and put the phone somewhere you have to stand up to reach.
items: Say out loud what you opened the app to do — most scrolls start with no errand at all.
Put the phone face down an arm's length away — a small distance breaks the reach-and-tap habit.
Turn off badges for the two worst apps — a red dot is a request you never agreed to.
Set a timer for the scroll instead of banning it — a known end makes stopping possible.
Swap the app on your home screen for a dull one — the thumb goes where the icon used to be.
Name the feeling that made you pick it up — boredom, dread and loneliness each want something different.
Read one long thing instead of twenty short ones — attention recovers when it is given somewhere to land.
Stand up and do one two-minute task — the loop breaks more easily through your body than your will.

title: The First Week in a New Place
description: For the days after a move, when the boxes are down but nothing feels like yours yet. It helps you make one room livable, learn the streets around you, and get a few ordinary routines going before homesickness sets in.
items: Finish one room before opening another box — one done space is somewhere to retreat to.
Make the bed properly on the first night — sleep is harder everywhere else in a new place.
Walk ten minutes in each direction from the door — streets stop being strange once you have used them.
Find the nearest grocery store and go once — the first errand turns an address into a neighborhood.
Put up two things that were on your old walls — familiar objects settle a room faster than new ones.
Message one person back home with a photo — being seen here helps here feel real.
Keep one routine exactly as it was — the same coffee or the same walk steadies the rest.
Say out loud that missing the old place is fine — homesickness is not a sign you chose wrong.

title: When Your Birthday Lands Hard
description: For the birthday that brings more dread than celebration, whether it is the number, who is missing, or the gap between the year you wanted and the one you had. It helps you take the day back on your own terms.
items: Decide a week ahead what the day will hold — a plan you made beats a day that happens to you.
Tell one person what you actually want from it — people guess badly and mean well.
Turn off the notifications if the messages sting — you can read them later, all at once.
Write down three things this year held — a hard year is rarely an empty one.
Do one thing you would want on an ordinary day — pleasure counts even when the date is loaded.
Name who is missing from the table out loud — an absence nobody mentions takes up more room.
Skip the comparison to where you thought you would be — that measure was invented, the day is real.
Let the day end early if it needs to — a short birthday is allowed.

title: The Week After Losing Your Job
description: For the first days after a layoff or a firing, before the job search begins in earnest. It helps you file the paperwork that matters, keep some shape to the day, and tell people in words that do not cost you anything.
items: File for unemployment in the first week — in most states the clock starts the day you apply.
Write down your last day and what you are owed — final pay and unused leave are easy to lose track of.
Check what happens to your health coverage — the gap is the part that catches people out.
Set a get-up time and keep it — a day with no edges is harder than a busy one.
Decide the one sentence you will tell people — having it ready saves you explaining it twelve times.
Keep one appointment outside the house each day — leaving the house stops the week from blurring.
Save the contacts and files you are allowed to — access tends to disappear sooner than you expect.
Give yourself a date to start applying — a planned pause is rest, an unplanned one is dread.

title: Eating When You Have No Appetite
description: For the stretches when food feels like a chore and meals get skipped without you deciding to. It helps you get something in without cooking, make eating less of an event, and notice when it is time to tell a doctor.
items: Keep something you can eat cold in the house — a meal that needs no cooking gets eaten.
Aim for something small every few hours — frequent and small beats waiting for hunger.
Drink it instead of chewing it — a smoothie or a glass of milk asks less of you.
Put it on a smaller plate — a full small plate is less daunting than a half-empty one.
Eat with someone, in person or on a call — company carries a meal that willpower will not.
Set a quiet alarm at the times you usually eat — appetite is a poor reminder right now.
Keep one food you always like within reach — familiar beats nutritious on the hard days.
Tell a doctor if this has run on for weeks — a long stretch is worth someone looking at.

title: When You Have Nothing Left for Work
description: For the stretch when the job has emptied you out and pushing harder is no longer working. It helps you find what to put down this week, ask for something concrete, and tell the difference between needing rest and needing a change.
items: List everything you are carrying at work — depletion is easier to argue with on paper.
Pick one thing to hand over or let slip this week — nothing changes while the load stays the same.
Name one concrete thing to ask your manager for — a specific ask is harder to wave away.
Take the leave you have already earned — unused days help nobody sitting in a system.
Stop checking messages after a set hour — the day needs an end you can point to.
Put one thing you enjoy back in the week — the first thing dropped is usually the one that refilled you.
Say out loud whether rest would fix this — some of it is tiredness and some of it is the job.
Tell one person outside work how it is going — this gets heavier when nobody else can see it.

title: When You Cannot Make the Decision
description: For the choice you have been turning over for weeks without landing anywhere. It helps you work out what you are actually weighing, set yourself a deadline, and make the call without needing certainty you are never going to get.
items: Write the decision as one plain question — half the stall is not knowing what is being asked.
Give yourself a date to decide by — an open choice takes up room until it has an end.
Name what you are afraid of either way — fear is usually the thing doing the deciding.
Write what you would tell a friend in this spot — advice comes out clearer for someone else.
Ask which option you can undo — a reversible choice needs far less thinking.
Decide what facts would actually change your mind — otherwise more research is only delay.
Tell one person which way you are leaning — saying it out loud tends to settle it.
Make the call and stop reopening it — rehearsing a settled choice costs more than living with it.

title: Getting Through a Family Visit
description: For the holiday weekend or the trip home where the old patterns are waiting. It helps you decide beforehand what you will and will not get into, build in time away from the room, and leave without a week of regret.
items: Decide the two topics you will not discuss — a line chosen in advance is easier to hold.
Book your own transport there and back — being able to leave changes the whole visit.
Pick an end time before you arrive — an open-ended visit runs until something goes wrong.
Have one sentence ready to change the subject — a prepared exit beats a clever answer.
Take a walk or an errand halfway through — twenty minutes out of the room resets a lot.
Text one person outside the family during the day — an outside voice keeps the room in proportion.
Pick one person you are glad to see — aiming the visit at them carries you through the rest.
Plan something easy for the evening you get back — the landing matters as much as the visit.

title: The Week You Are Waiting on News
description: For the stretch between a test, an application or a decision and the answer, when nothing you do changes the outcome. It helps you put the waiting somewhere, keep the days usable, and stop rehearsing every version of the result.
items: Find out when the answer actually comes — a known date is easier to wait out than an open one.
Set one time a day to check for it — all-day checking turns one wait into fifty.
Write the worst outcome and your first three steps — a plan makes the bad version survivable.
Stop researching once you have what you need — more reading rarely changes the answer.
Put something in the calendar for each day — an empty week fills up with the waiting.
Tell one person you are waiting — carrying it silently makes it heavier than it is.
Move your body once a day, even briefly — waiting sits in the body as much as the head.
Notice when you are rehearsing and name it — the fiftieth run-through tells you nothing new.
